textos.titulo: Contracts Data API v2 — Getting Started
paragrafos: The Contracts Data API provides registered applications with read-only access to procurement records published by participating agencies. All requests must be sent over HTTPS. Calls made over plain HTTP are rejected rather than redirected, so clients should not rely on automatic upgrades to a secure connection.

Authentication. Every request must include a bearer token in the Authorization header. Tokens are issued through the developer portal and expire 60 minutes after they are created. When a token expires, the API returns 401 Unauthorized, and the client is expected to obtain a new one with its refresh credential instead of asking the user to log in again. Each token is bound to a single application; sharing it with other applications violates the terms of use and may lead to the suspension of the account.

Pagination. List endpoints return at most 100 items per page. Instead of page numbers, the API uses cursor-based pagination: each response includes a next_cursor field, which must be sent unchanged in the following request. When next_cursor is null, there are no further results. Cursors are opaque strings, and clients should not attempt to decode or build them, since their internal format may change without notice.

Rate limiting. Each application may send up to 600 requests per minute. Every response carries the headers X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset, which indicate how many calls are left in the current window and when it will be renewed. If the limit is exceeded, the server responds with 429 Too Many Requests and includes a Retry-After header. Clients should wait at least the number of seconds indicated before trying again; retrying immediately in a tight loop will only extend the block.

Versioning. Version 1 of the API was deprecated in March and will eventually be shut down. Although it still answers requests, it no longer receives bug fixes, and new integrations should target version 2 only.

1. Introduction. This document defines a common format for audit events generated by systems that process financial records. Its purpose is to allow logs produced by different vendors to be collected, correlated and preserved by a single archiving service. The transport of events between systems is outside the scope of this document and is addressed in a separate specification.

2. Conventions. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY indicate requirement levels. An implementation that fails to satisfy a MUST requirement is not compliant, whereas an implementation that ignores a SHOULD requirement may still be compliant, provided that it has a valid reason and documents that reason. MAY identifies a truly optional feature.

3. Event Structure. Each event MUST contain a timestamp, an actor identifier, an action code and an outcome. Timestamps MUST be expressed in UTC using the ISO 8601 format and SHOULD include milliseconds. The actor identifier MUST NOT contain personal data, such as names or national identification numbers; producers SHOULD instead use a pseudonymous reference that only authorized staff can resolve. Producers MAY add custom fields, but these MUST be placed under the ext object so that they do not collide with fields defined in future revisions.

4. Integrity. Once written, an event MUST NOT be modified. Corrections are made by appending a new event that references the original one. Archiving services SHOULD verify the hash chain of each batch upon receipt and MUST reject any batch in which a gap is detected, unless the producer has previously declared a maintenance window covering that interval.

5. Security Considerations. Because audit logs frequently become targets after an intrusion, access to them SHOULD be restricted to read-only roles. Implementers are reminded that compliance with this format does not, by itself, guarantee that the recorded events are accurate.

Summary. On 14 May, between 09:12 and 10:47 UTC, the citizen payment portal was unavailable for approximately 95 minutes. During this period, users who tried to issue payment slips received a generic error page. No data was lost, and no transaction was processed twice. This report follows a blameless format: its goal is to understand what happened and how to prevent it from happening again, not to assign individual fault.

Root cause. The incident began shortly after a routine deployment that introduced a new connection pool setting. The change reduced the maximum number of database connections from 200 to 20, a value that had actually been intended for the staging environment only. Under normal morning traffic, the pool was exhausted within minutes, and requests started to time out. Although the deployment pipeline ran all automated tests successfully, none of them simulated production load, so the error went unnoticed.

Detection and response. Monitoring alerts fired at 09:19, but responders initially classified them as a network problem, since similar symptoms had been observed during a provider failure the previous week. This assumption delayed the investigation by about 40 minutes. Once the on-call engineer correlated the alerts with the deployment, the team decided to roll back the release, which restored the service at 10:47.

Lessons learned. First, configuration values that differ between environments must be validated during deployment, not only during code review. Second, our runbook did not require responders to check recent changes before investigating infrastructure, which it now does. Finally, we will set up a load testing stage in the pipeline and phase out manual edits to configuration files by the end of the quarter.

textos.titulo: Group-Level Evaluation of Document Classifiers Used in Public Audits
textos.genero: resumo (abstract) de artigo científico de IA
paragrafos: Background. Public oversight bodies increasingly rely on machine learning models to screen large volumes of documents, such as invoices and procurement notices, and to flag those that deserve closer inspection. While these tools can reduce manual workload, little is known about how consistently they perform across different types of issuers, particularly small municipalities, whose documents are often scanned at low resolution.

Methods. We evaluated three text classification models on a dataset of 48,000 documents labeled by experienced auditors. Rather than reporting a single accuracy figure, we measured precision and recall separately for each group of issuers, defined by population size and level of digitization. We also tested whether the models relied on spurious features, such as the presence of a particular letterhead, by systematically removing those features from the input.

Results. All models achieved an overall accuracy above 91%. However, recall for documents from small municipalities was up to 18 percentage points lower than for documents from state agencies, which means that irregular documents from these issuers were more likely to go unflagged. The gap was largely explained by optical character recognition errors rather than by the classifiers themselves. When the letterhead was removed, the performance of one model dropped sharply, suggesting that it had learned to associate certain layouts with risk.

Conclusions. These findings indicate that a high aggregate score may conceal significant disparities between groups. We argue that evaluation reports for audit tools should present results disaggregated by relevant groups and that human review should remain mandatory for low-confidence predictions. Future work will assess whether improving image quality is sufficient to close the gap.

textos.titulo: e-Docs Desktop Client — User Guide, Chapter 3: Signing and Submitting Documents
paragrafos: This chapter explains how to sign documents digitally and submit them to a case file. Before you begin, make sure that your digital certificate is installed and that the card reader, if you use one, is connected to your computer. The client will not display the Sign button unless a valid certificate is detected.

To sign a document, open the case file, select the document in the Attachments panel and click Sign. You will then be asked to enter your certificate PIN. If you enter an incorrect PIN three times in a row, the certificate will be locked, and you will have to contact the issuing authority to unlock it. The client cannot reset the PIN on your behalf.

Signed documents cannot be edited. If you need to change the content of a document after signing it, upload a new version and sign it again. The previous version remains in the file history, which ensures that every change can be traced. Note: deleting a signed document is only possible while the case file is still in draft status.

When all documents are ready, click Submit. The client checks every file before sending it: only PDF files of up to 25 MB are accepted, and password-protected files are rejected, since the server would be unable to index their contents. A receipt is then generated. Keep it until the submission appears in the case history, which may take up to ten minutes.

Tip: if you often work with large batches, you can set up a watched folder under Settings > Automation. Files placed in this folder are attached to the selected case file automatically; however, they still have to be signed one by one.

textos.titulo: Security Advisory SA-2026-07: Authentication Bypass in Tollbridge Gateway
paragrafos: Summary. A vulnerability has been identified in the administration console of Tollbridge Gateway, versions 3.2.0 through 3.4.1. An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the console can bypass the login check by sending a request with a crafted X-Forwarded-User header, which makes the console treat the attacker as an already authenticated administrator. In other words, the attacker can pretend to be a legitimate user without knowing any password. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to change routing rules and read stored credentials. The issue has been rated Critical.

Impact. Installations in which the console is reachable only from an isolated management network are less exposed; nevertheless, they remain vulnerable to attackers who have already gained a foothold inside that network. We are not aware of any active exploitation at the time of publication. However, given how easily the flaw can be reproduced, we expect proof-of-concept code to become public soon.

Remediation. Administrators should upgrade to version 3.4.2, which fixes the issue, as soon as possible. Unless an immediate upgrade is feasible, the console should be disabled or restricted to trusted IP addresses as a temporary workaround. Note that the workaround does not remove the vulnerability; it only reduces the attack surface.

Detection. To determine whether a system may have been compromised, administrators can search the access logs for requests to the /admin path that contain the X-Forwarded-User header with an empty value. Any change to routing rules that cannot be matched to an authorized change ticket should be treated as suspicious, and all credentials stored in the gateway should be rotated.

Version 5.0 is a major release focused on performance and security. Because it contains breaking changes, we recommend reading these notes in full before upgrading production environments. Users of version 4.x can upgrade in place, but earlier versions must first be upgraded to 4.9.

New features. Parallel transfers are now enabled by default, which reduces synchronization time by up to 40% on large repositories. A new --dry-run flag shows which files would be changed without actually changing them. The tool also supports authentication through short-lived tokens issued by external identity providers.

Breaking changes. The sync-all command has been removed; use sync --recursive instead. Configuration files in the legacy INI format are no longer read. Run datasync migrate-config to convert them to YAML before upgrading; otherwise, the tool will start with default settings and may ignore your exclusion rules.

Deprecations. Password-based authentication is deprecated and will be removed in version 6.0. It still works in this release, but a warning is displayed every time it is used. We also plan to phase out support for TLS 1.1 over the next two minor releases.

Fixed and known issues. A memory leak that occurred when synchronizing directories with more than one million files has been fixed. On some network file systems, timestamps may be reported incorrectly; this issue does not affect data integrity. If you run into problems after upgrading, you can roll back to 4.9 by reinstalling the previous package, since version 5.0 does not change the format of existing repositories.

textos.titulo: Managed Database Service — Backups and High Availability
paragrafos: The managed database service protects your data through two complementary mechanisms: automated backups and high availability (HA). It is important to understand that they address different risks. Backups allow you to recover data that has been deleted or corrupted, whereas HA keeps the database running when the underlying infrastructure fails.

Automated backups are enabled by default and run once a day during a maintenance window of your choice. In addition, transaction logs are archived every five minutes, which allows point-in-time recovery to any moment within the retention period. The default retention period is seven days and can be extended to up to 35 days. Backups are stored in a different zone from the primary instance; however, they remain in the same region unless you enable cross-region copies.

When HA is enabled, the service maintains a standby replica in another availability zone and replicates every write to it synchronously. If the primary instance becomes unavailable, the service promotes the standby automatically, usually within 60 to 120 seconds. Applications should connect through the instance endpoint rather than through IP addresses, since the endpoint is updated to point to the new primary after a failover.

The standby replica cannot be used to serve read traffic. If you need to offload queries, create a read replica instead. Read replicas are updated asynchronously and may therefore lag slightly behind the primary. Note also that HA does not protect against logical errors: if a user drops a table, the deletion is replicated to the standby within milliseconds.

Enabling HA roughly doubles the compute cost of an instance. For production workloads, we nevertheless recommend combining HA with backups and testing restores periodically, because a backup that has never been restored cannot be considered reliable.

textos.titulo: Data Retention and Access Policy — Internal Analytics Platform
textos.genero: política de governança de dados e privacidade
paragrafos: Purpose and scope. This policy establishes how personal data is collected, stored and accessed on the internal analytics platform. It applies to all employees, contractors and third-party service providers who handle data on behalf of the organization, regardless of where they are located.

Principles. Personal data shall be collected only for specified and legitimate purposes and shall not be further processed in ways that are incompatible with those purposes. Teams shall request only the fields they actually need; access to complete datasets will not be granted merely because it is more convenient. Where possible, personal identifiers must be pseudonymized before the data is loaded into the analytics environment.

Access control. Access is granted on a least-privilege basis and must be approved by the data owner, who is accountable for the dataset, rather than by the data steward, whose role is to maintain its quality and documentation. Access rights are reviewed every six months, and those that are no longer justified are revoked. Contractors' access expires automatically at the end of their contract unless it is formally renewed.

Retention. Personal data shall be retained only for as long as necessary to fulfil the purpose for which it was collected. When the retention period ends, records must be deleted or anonymized. Anonymized data may be kept indefinitely, provided that individuals can no longer be identified, either directly or by combining it with other available information.

Incidents and compliance. Any suspected breach must be reported to the data protection officer within 24 hours of its discovery, even if its impact is still unclear. Failure to comply with this policy may result in disciplinary action. This policy will be reviewed annually or whenever relevant legislation changes.

textos.titulo: Beyond Dashboards: Making Observability Work for Small Teams
textos.genero: artigo técnico sobre DevOps e observabilidade
paragrafos: Many teams assume that observability is simply a new name for monitoring. Monitoring, however, answers questions that were defined in advance: is the server up? Is the disk almost full? Observability goes further. It is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system by examining the data it produces, even when the problem is one that nobody anticipated.

This data is usually described in terms of three signals: metrics, logs and traces. Metrics are numerical measurements aggregated over time, which makes them cheap to store and well suited to alerting. Logs record discrete events in detail, while traces follow a single request as it travels through multiple services. None of these signals is sufficient on its own; their value comes from the ability to move from one to another during an investigation.

A common mistake is to alert on every metric that can be collected. When engineers receive dozens of notifications a day, they eventually start ignoring them, a phenomenon known as alert fatigue. A better approach is to alert on symptoms that users actually experience, such as error rates and latency, and to define service level objectives (SLOs) that make clear how much failure is acceptable.

Small teams do not need to adopt every tool at once. They can start by adding structured logs and a correlation ID to each request, which already makes it possible to connect events across services. Tracing can then be introduced gradually, beginning with the most critical paths. Open standards such as OpenTelemetry help teams avoid vendor lock-in, since the same instrumentation can send data to different back ends.

Ultimately, observability is less about tools than about culture. Unless teams regularly use their telemetry to ask new questions, even the most sophisticated platform will become just another set of dashboards that no one looks at.
